import cv2

Part 1: Image Manipulation¶

You are given some code below. Can you explain 2 important things that are happening in this code? Write youe answer in the cell right after this cell

In [2]:
# Download the Lena image
!wget https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/7/7d/Lenna_%28test_image%29.png -O lena.png


# Read the image
img = cv2.imread('lena.png')

#
resized_img = cv2.resize(img, (img.shape[1] // 5, img.shape[0] // 5))

# Convert from BGR to RGB for displaying using matplotlib

plt.imshow(resized_img_rgb)

plt.axis('off')

# Show the images
plt.show()

Answer to Part 1¶

There are three important things happening in this cell¶

  1. The picture is being resized
  2. The original picture is being converted to RGB

Part 3: Binarization¶

In Part 3, you will read an image and binarize it Here are the instructions:

  1. Read the image
  2. Print the shape of this image
  3. Binarize this image by writing a custom function. This custom function should take the image as input, then only consider the red plane of the image (you will need to use numpy)
  4. Use threshold values of 128, 150 and 240. Display this image side by side with the original image
  5. Now binarize this image using any one of the libraries.
  6. Display this image side by side the original image. Which method did you like the best and why?
In [5]:
# Download the Lena image
!wget https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/7/7d/Lenna_%28test_image%29.png -O lena.png

# Read the image
img = cv2.imread('lena.png')

# Convert from BGR to RGB for displaying using matplotlib
img_rgb = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)

#print shape of img
print(img.shape)

#binarize function
def binarize(img, threshold):
  #convert image to only having red plane
  red_img = img[:,:,0]
  binary_image = np.zeros_like(red_img)
  #binarize image
  binary_img = np.where(red_img > threshold, 255, 0)
  return binary_img

# Use threshold values of 128, 150, 240
binary_img1 = binarize(img_rgb, 128)
binary_img2 = binarize(img_rgb, 150)
binary_img3 = binarize(img_rgb, 240)

#Display all images side by side with the original img
plt.subplot(2, 3, 1)
plt.imshow(img_rgb)
plt.title('Original Image')
plt.axis('off')

plt.subplot(2, 3, 2)
plt.imshow(binary_img1, cmap='gray')
plt.title('Binary Image 1')
plt.axis('off')

plt.subplot(2, 3, 3)
plt.imshow(binary_img2, cmap='gray')
plt.title('Binary Image 2')
plt.axis('off')

plt.subplot(2, 3, 4)
plt.imshow(binary_img3, cmap='gray')
plt.title('Binary Image 3')
plt.axis('off')

plt.show()

Part 4: Grayscale Conversion¶

In Part 4, you will read an image and convert it to grayscale Here are the instructions:

  1. Read the image
  2. Print the shape of this image
  3. Convert this image to grayscale by writing a custom averaging function. You will need to run a for loop through each colored plane and and take the average for each pixel.
  4. Display this image.
    NOTE: this question might be a little bit different than what you have seen in the module. You need to be be able to do this with for loops and numpy for full credit
In [7]:
# Download the Lena image
!wget https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/7/7d/Lenna_%28test_image%29.png -O lena.png

# Read the image
img = cv2.imread('lena.png')

# Convert from BGR to RGB for displaying using matplotlib
img_rgb = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)

#print shape of img
print(img.shape)

#Convert image to Grayscale using custom averaging function
def grayscale(img):
  height, width, _ = img.shape
  #loop through each colored plane and take the avg
  gray_img = np.zeros((img.shape[0], img.shape[1]), dtype=np.uint8)
  for i in range(height):
        for j in range(width):
            # Get R, G, B values for the pixel
            r, g, b = img[i, j]
            # Compute average of R, G, B
            avg = (int(r) + int(g) + int(b)) // 3
            # Assign average to grayscale image
            gray_img[i, j] = avg
  return gray_img
#test function
gray_img = grayscale(img_rgb)

#Display image
plt.imshow(gray_img, cmap='gray')
plt.title('Grayscale Image')
plt.axis('off')
plt.show()
